doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Rock and roll and the decline of jazz work
title: Big bands shrink to small groups
summary: Ellington sidemen and Basie's small group at the Champagne Supper Club; Woody Herman, Buddy Rich and Kirk in 1960 Chicago.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Sure, he had the small group in the fifties.
With Clark Terry and Wardell and Buddy DeFranco and Sam Jones I think on bass.
I think Jimmy Lewis played bass.
Oh Jimmy Lewis, I beg your pardon, yeah Jimmy Lewis. And Basie of course and Gus Johnson. Yeah they played at the Champagne Supper Club here in San Francisco, small

group. So that’s what it did with us. The big bands, they had to reduce. Woody Herman was out with a small group. Buddy Rich was out with a quintet. In ’60, when we were in Chicago, he was playing in the room under our hotel. The Cloisters. We stayed at the Maryland Hotel. And they had a room called The Cloisters. Buddy Rich came in, Miles, he played at the Bird House but they stayed at the hotel. And Rahsaan Roland Kirk, they used to lead him around with all these horns around his neck, in 1960, before he made the big time. But that’s what happened. Small groups. And even the singing groups, they had to lobby Congress to reduce that 20% entertainment tax. Because if they were singing then you had to pay entertainment tax. That was wartime tax. They taxed all entertainment.
